claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid, homogeneous, and crystalline, with minimal surface-composition variation.
Preferential surface segregation governs the onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Preferential surface segregation produces a local melting-point depression at nanoparticle surfaces.
Melting begins through premelting at the nanoparticle surface.
The surface-melted region propagates inward as temperature increases.
Atomic segregation occurs at grain boundaries and at the nanoparticle exterior.
Segregated surface regions have a lower local melting point than the bulk or particle core.
Atoms in segregated surface regions become disordered at a lower temperature than atoms in the core.
Surface premelting acts as a nucleation site for continued phase transition.
The onset temperature for melting is lower at the nanoparticle surface than in the core.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation exhibit more pronounced surface-initiated, inward-progressing melting.
Nanoparticles with a more uniform elemental distribution have a higher melting-onset temperature than nanoparticles with pronounced surface segregation.
Nanoparticles with a more uniform elemental distribution melt more uniformly across the particle.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to nanoparticle sizes for which surface-to-volume effects significantly influence thermal behavior.
Particles below approximately 30 nm have a sufficiently significant surface-to-volume ratio for the proposed comparison.
An inert or vacuum atmosphere avoids oxidation during the thermal experiment.
